guidance:
Read only Table 1. Ignore all other tables, figures, footnotes, and text.

1) Columns and headers
- Identify the full header structure at the top of Table 1.
- Include every explicit header that represents a data column (e.g., each group of participants or condition) in the `columns` list.
- If there are stacked or nested headers (a top-level group above several subcolumns), do NOT treat the group row as a separate column. Instead, join the group and the leaf header into one unique label like "<group>: <leaf>" and use that as `column_label`.
- The leftmost column that lists the row names may have a heading (e.g., "Characteristic" or similar). If it has a heading, include that heading in `columns`, but do not create any cells for it; its entries are captured in `row_label`.
- Every `column_label` you use in cells must appear exactly once in `columns`.

2) Row labels and row groups
- Read the table from top to bottom and distinguish:
  • Section or category headings (usually bold, centered, or spanning multiple columns).
  • Actual data rows (usually aligned with column entries).
- A section or category heading that groups several subsequent rows becomes `row_group`. Use the heading text verbatim.
- For each data row within a section, use the text in the leftmost label column as `row_label`, and the section heading as `row_group`.
- If a data row is not clearly under any section heading, set `row_group` to null.
- If the table reports a summary statistic directly on a section heading (i.e., the heading itself has values in data columns on the same row), represent it with `row_group` equal to the section heading text and `row_label` = null.
- Do not invert row_group and row_label. The category heading is row_group; the individual items under it are row_label.

3) Cells and values
- Create one cell object for every non-empty intersection of a data row and a data column.
- Each cell must have exactly: `row_label`, `row_group`, `column_label`, and `value`.
- Copy each value exactly as shown, including punctuation, signs, units, parentheses, ranges, thousands separators, and textual symbols (e.g., percentages, N/A, dashes used as values).
- Do not create a cell for an empty source cell. Never invent values. Do not use null, empty strings, or whitespace-only strings as values.
- A printed zero is a real value and must be captured.

4) Avoiding missing and extra cells
- Check systematically that every visible numeric or textual entry in the body of Table 1 is represented once as a cell with matching row_group, row_label, and column_label.
- Do not create cells for heading rows that contain no data values.
- Do not introduce additional totals or combined columns beyond what appears in the header. Only use columns that are explicitly defined by the table.
- Do not move data between categories: ensure that values appearing in a given section heading and row name remain associated with that same `row_group` and `row_label`.
- For each row, verify that you have cells for all columns that show a value on that row, and no cells for columns that are blank on that row.

5) Uniqueness and consistency
- Do not emit duplicate cells. A particular combination of (`row_group`, `row_label`, `column_label`) must appear at most once.
- Keep spelling, capitalization, and symbols in `row_group`, `row_label`, and `column_label` consistent with the table text.
- If the same section heading appears multiple times, use exactly the same `row_group` string for those rows.

Apply these rules uniformly to all Table 1 layouts, even if the formatting is complex or irregular.
